h: Visiting Kindly, Then Exploring the Fine City
p: A sanctuary visit works a little differently from a trip to a farm park or zoo. The animals here aren't on show for entertainment; they're living out their lives somewhere safe, and the people who care for them put their wellbeing first. That's worth explaining to children before you go, because it turns the day into something more thoughtful. Kids often respond brilliantly when they realise every animal has a name and a past, and many come home asking how they can help.

Being a donation-funded charity, small things make a big difference, whether that's popping a few coins in a collection box, browsing a charity shop or simply sharing your photos and telling friends. Dress for fields and farm tracks, keep dogs at home unless you've been told otherwise, and give yourself time to stand and watch rather than rushing from paddock to paddock.

If you're heading for the coastal site at West Runton, you're in a spot with serious prehistoric credentials. In 1990 the remains of a huge steppe mammoth were found in the cliffs here, a remarkably complete skeleton that caused quite a stir. The village also sits beside Beeston Bump, a hill with great views along the coast towards Sheringham.

Back in Norwich, swap the obvious sights for a few hidden gems. Elm Hill is a gorgeous cobbled street of Tudor buildings that looks straight out of a costume drama, while Norwich Market, with its stripy-roofed stalls, has been trading in the city centre for centuries and is a cracking place for lunch. The Plantation Garden, a restored Victorian garden tucked away in an old quarry, is a peaceful little secret just outside the city centre.
